articles.title: How UN chief Antonio Guterres tests the limits of quiet diplomacy
articles.summary: Portugal's ex-PM seeks to resolve crises via patient negotiation, but success relies on leaders' willingness to act.
articles.preview: Portugal's Prime Minister Antonio Guterres called President Bill Clinton from Lisbon on August 30 and September 8, 1999, to discuss the growing crisis in East Timor. The small Southeast Asian territory, which had endured a brutal Indonesian occupation since 1975, was again engulfed in violence after voters overwhelmingly chose independence in a referendum.
articles.body:
Portugal's Prime Minister Antonio Guterres called President Bill Clinton from Lisbon on August 30 and September 8, 1999, to discuss the growing crisis in East Timor. The small Southeast Asian territory, which had endured a brutal Indonesian occupation since 1975, was again engulfed in violence after voters overwhelmingly chose independence in a referendum. Pro-Indonesian militias responded to the vote for independence by unleashing a so-called "scorched-earth" campaign, destroying infrastructure, displacing up to half a million people and killing thousands.

The crisis resonated in Portugal, where linguistic, Catholic, and historical ties to its former colony helped fuel a solidarity movement. An estimated 10,000 demonstrators, dressed in white, formed human chains through Lisbon’s city streets.

Guterres had raised the issue before. At a 1996 summit in Bangkok, he met Indonesia’s President Suharto and broached the politically sensitive topic of East Timor, offering to restore diplomatic relations (severed since the 1975 invasion) in exchange for the release of Timorese resistance leader Xanana Gusmao. The proposal was met with an awkward silence.

This time, Guterres was asking the United States to support a UN mission in East Timor, but Washington was reluctant to confront Indonesia. Guterres recalled in his 2022 biography, “Honest Broker”, that he warned Clinton during the second call that Portugal could reconsider its Balkan deployments if the international community failed to intervene. Portugal’s contribution to NATO was small but politically well-placed, with its troops serving in the alliance’s prominent post-Cold War missions in Bosnia and Kosovo.

Guterres offered Clinton a choice: risk a public falling-out with a founding NATO ally, or use Washington’s influence to make Indonesia accept an international force in East Timor. The next day, amid growing international pressure, the White House stated that Indonesia “must” allow international assistance.

For Guterres, it was an early test of multilateral crisis diplomacy, a skill set he would later bring to his post as UN secretary-general in 2017. East Timor, also known as Timor-Leste, finally won its freedom in 2002. For spearheading diplomatic efforts during the 1999 crisis, Guterres was awarded Timorese citizenship in 2024.

“Antonio Guterres pushed a lot for what we now call the referendum, and when violence broke out he was one of the people calling for a UN intervention,” said Christine Cabasset, a teacher at Lille Catholic University and an expert on East Timor, reflecting on how the East Timor crisis foreshadowed Guterres’s later career.

“Guterres had a critical role all along the way,” she added, noting how he later pushed for the creation of the UN Transitional Administration in East Timor.

“There is also a kind of love story with the UN, I mean, that strong link between Timor-Leste and the UN… Multilateralism, which is still really the purpose of the UN, has been critical in the independence of Timor-Leste. And Guterres [himself] became very important in the UN starting from 2005.”

Guterres’s response to the East Timor crisis reflected an approach shaped by his Catholic faith, his early work with Portugal’s poor and his political coming of age after the fall of a dictatorship. He carried those experiences into a career built on finding common ground and helping people caught in crises. But as UN secretary-general, he has faced the limits of that approach, struggling to turn appeals for peace into action when the world’s most powerful countries are at odds.

A revolution of flowers

Antonio Manuel de Oliveira Guterres was born in Lisbon on April 30, 1949, to Ilda Candida de Oliveira Guterres and Virgilio Dias Guterres, a senior employee of the Lisbon gas and electricity company. He spent summers and extended periods in the countryside with his grandparents in the small village of Donas. His childhood friend Vitor Dias told the newspaper Publico that Guterres’s grandmother stressed the importance of education and by “three or four years old, he already knew how to write his name.” The grandparents’ house was right next to the church where “Little Toni” often served as an altar boy.

Portugal was then under the rule of dictator Antonio Salazar, whose Estado Novo regime closely resembled Italian fascism, but with less emphasis on brute force, personality cults and revolutionary zeal, and more on Catholic conservatism. As a result, the country was politically and culturally cut off from much of democratic Western Europe.

“As dictator, [Salazar] was very much marked by corporatism, the idea of an organic society without conflict and also by Roman Catholic conservative values,” said Antonio Costa Pinto, a historian at the University of Lisbon.

“But especially in the late 60s and early 70s … it basically became a Cold War dictatorship, an anti-communist one.”

Among the regime’s core beliefs was that the seafaring Portuguese were innately suited to colonialism and it stubbornly clung to the centuries-old Portuguese empire, fighting bloody rebellions in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau.

“We were a very closed country. We had censorship everywhere. We had the political police,” remembered Joao Goulao, a retired Portuguese doctor who grew up in that era.

“There was a very limited mobility of citizens; we were not able to travel abroad without a lot of formalities. We were not a very sexy destination for tourism, so people didn’t come to us and we were very isolated.”

Still, Portugal was a founding member of NATO, a US ally and a participant in Western economic institutions.

“In the late 60s especially, there was a huge contradiction between the type of censorship and the type of values – very conservative – supported by the dictatorship and the structure of Portuguese society that was already much more modern,” said Costa Pinto.

“There was a contradiction between the values of the political elite and the values of a more developed, educated middle class.”

Portuguese citizens saw those contradictions in everyday life: Coca-Cola was banned from being made in Portugal, and until 1970, anyone who owned a cigarette lighter needed an annual licence — a regulation imposed to protect the national match industry.

Although literacy rates improved under Salazar, outside the major cities, many Portuguese children received only minimal schooling from teachers who often had only had a fourth-grade education themselves. The instructors’ main qualification was loyalty to the regime.

But Guterres’ grandmother’s efforts to ensure he had a proper education paid off. He earned top marks at his high school in Lisbon and was reportedly recognised with a national academic prize in 1965. The future statesman went on to study electrical engineering at Lisbon’s Instituto Superior Tecnico, graduating in 1971.

While there, Guterres led the university’s Social Action Centre, which conducted social work in the capital’s poorest neighbourhoods. He also joined the Grupo da Luz (Group of Light), a Catholic student club led by Father Vitor Melicias, who became a close personal friend and confidant.

Although the Group of Light never directly challenged the regime, Melicias told World Mission Magazine that its members regularly changed meeting locations to avoid attracting the attention of the secret police.

Even before university, Guterres’s faith impacted his views on social work and volunteerism. He was especially inspired by the Second Vatican Council of 1962-1965, which affirmed the Church’s commitment to human rights and encouraged everyone to play an active role in society. In 1967, at age 18, he joined the mass movement to help victims of the catastrophic Lisbon flash floods, which had killed hundreds. The regime, meanwhile, worked to conceal the scale of the disaster.

“There was a huge mobilisation, especially of students – not just Catholics – to support the shantytowns that had been flooded in the suburbs of Lisbon and the Tagus River,” explained Costa Pinto.

“Many of the students became politicised against the dictatorship as another effect of this huge movement to support the poor shantytowns.”

Guterres met his soon-to-be wife, Luisa Amelia Guimaraes e Melo, through the Catholic University Youth movement, according to his biography. The couple wed in 1972 — Father Melicias officiated — and went on to have two children, Pedro and Mariana. Guterres said it was his wife, a child psychiatrist, who shared a valuable lesson with him that proved useful in his international diplomacy.

“She taught me something that was extremely useful for all my political activities. When two people are together, they are not two but six. What each one is, what each one thinks he or she is and what each one thinks the other is,” he said at a 2016 debate hosted by the Guardian newspaper.

“And what is true for people is also true for countries and organisations. One of the roles of the secretary-general … is to [ensure] that misunderstandings disappear and the false perceptions disappear. Perceptions are essential in politics,” Guterres said.

Salazar fell ill and was removed from office in 1968, dying two years later. The Estado Novo survived under his successor, Marcelo Caetano, until 1974. Disillusioned with the colonial wars, a cadre of military officers mounted a coup and seized control of the government on April 25 that year. Crowds flooded the streets to rally behind the mutineers, and women stuck red carnations in soldiers’ rifle barrels, begging them not to kill. The Carnation Revolution, as it became known, set Portugal on a whole new course.

“There was a complete change, a sudden openness in our society,” said Goulao, who was 20 at the time.

“We started to have the right to speak about our problems, without censorship in the press,” he explained. Portugal’s citizens were also suddenly able to travel abroad, which he had never done before. This inspired Goulao to buy an Interrail train pass and travel throughout the continent. “I travelled through Europe and I saw things I’d never have guessed. Portugal became fashionable, so we started to have lots of people visiting us.”

That period immediately after the coup also saw a tense revolutionary upheaval, said Costa Pinto, with some fearing that Portugal could fall to a reactionary counter-coup or a communist takeover. But by 1975, more moderate forces prevailed and the country became yet another West European-style democracy.

In 1974, Guterres joined the Socialist Party (PS) and grew a moustache in tribute to Chile’s overthrown left-wing President Salvador Allende.

“I didn’t have significant political activity before the 25th of April [of 1974],” he said in a 2016 interview with journalist Anabela Mota Ribeiro.

“My involvement was in social issues. I slowly, through that, awakened to political options,” he said.

In 1976, the young engineer was elected to parliament to represent Castelo Branco in Portugal’s first democratic election.

Becoming prime minister

During his years in the PS, Guterres sat on several government committees.

Foreshadowing his future career, he cofounded the Portuguese Refugee Council in 1991, which prioritised fighting discrimination and inequality for asylum seekers.

That same year, the PS lost the general election to the centre-right Social Democrats (PSD), whose leader, Prime Minister Anibal Cavaco Silva, had presided over years of stable economic growth.

“I’m in shock!” Guterres told reporters on election night. The remark dealt a blow to PS leader Jorge Sampaio and helped set the stage for a leadership challenge. Guterres took over the party the following year. He then set about recasting the PS as a moderate, modern European social-democratic party that could appeal beyond its traditional base.

The party revised its imagery, pairing its clenched fist with the rose associated with European social democracy, part of Guterres’s push to soften the party’s militant image and present it as a credible alternative.

“His priority and leadership style were basically very respectful to democratic institutions,” observed Costa Pinto. “There were no elements of the typical populist type of approach to politics.”

The same year, Guterres was also elected vice president of the Socialist International, a global organisation of social-democratic, socialist and labour parties.

Campaigning under the slogan “heart and reason”, Guterres narrowly won the 1995 Portuguese election and became prime minister of a minority government. Governing without a parliamentary majority required him to build support, issue by issue, reinforcing a consensus-building style. Costa Pinto traces that approach to the Catholic activism that shaped Guterres long before he got into politics.

“The main skeleton, let’s say, of Guterres’ political activity is political Catholicism,” said Costa Pinto. “He is on the centre-left, social democratic party, but he is always very keen on two specific dimensions. The first is the social dimension of democracy, redistribution, support of the poor and that comes from his early activism as a young Catholic during the last phase of the dictatorship. And the second, of course, is Catholicism.”

A practising Catholic, Guterres stood out in the Socialist Party, whose early membership included many secular activists and former Marxists. His beliefs were put to the test in 1997 when his own party proposed to legalise abortion. He faced internal pressure from his own MPs to support the law, but Guterres held firm and refused. But that was not the end of it.

The issue went to a referendum the following year, and Guterres allowed socialist MPs a free vote. Although his party backed the reform, the prime minister said he personally opposed it and stayed out of the campaign. The proposal was narrowly rejected, but turnout was low.

“It failed because the main party of the centre-left did not mobilise and that's because Guterres was the leader of the party,” Costa Pinto explained.

Portugal finally legalised abortion after a second referendum in 2007, long after Guterres had left office.

In early 1998, Guterres suffered a profound personal loss. His wife Luisa, who had been gravely ill for years, died after a serious relapse despite having undergone a liver transplant. She had been receiving treatment at a clinic in London.

Another pressing social issue for his government was drugs. While the dictatorship had kept Portugal closed to the world, narcotics came flooding in after the 1974 revolution.

“Everybody wanted to experiment with something new that came with freedom,” Goulao, who ran a network of addiction clinics, told Al Jazeera.

“Heroin became very popular and spread rapidly among all the social groups in our society. [Then] in the beginning of the 1980s, AIDS came along to complicate things.”

By the 1990s, an estimated one percent of the population was hooked on heroin and the country had one of the highest rates of HIV infection among people who injected drugs in the European Union. In 1998, Guterres appointed Goulao to an expert panel exploring solutions to that crisis.

“It’s important to say that Guterres paid a lot of attention to this area,” Goulao recalled.

“We had some proximity because his sister was a psychiatrist who used to work in this area at the time. So we had a direct line to pass along our concerns, and he was very attentive,” he explained.

The panel recommended decriminalisation: drug dealers remained criminals, but catching their clientele was no longer a priority for police. Instead, someone with a dose in their pocket would be sent before a panel that warned them of the dangers and connected them with health services if necessary, after which they were free to leave. The goal was to stop punishing addicts and to stop wasting resources on casual consumers.

The policy changes worked. Despite fears that Portugal would become a drug den attracting addicts worldwide, the number of serious addicts, fatal overdoses and HIV infections dropped dramatically after the reforms of 2001. The number of new annual HIV infections among drug users fell from 907 in 2000 to 267 by 2008.

“He’s very nice and a good listener and he is very easy to approach and to discuss issues with,” Goulao said of Guterres’s style, noting how the UN chief has faced difficult decisions and had to take in advice from a broad group while trying to find consensus.

But this accommodating approach has not always worked.

Pedro Ferraz da Costa, who headed the Confederation of Portuguese Industry (CIP) at the time, described Guterres as having “intelligence and quick thinking,” but noted how his determination to build consensus was sometimes detrimental.

“He likes everyone to like him so much that it makes it impossible for him to make decisions,” Ferraz da Costa told TV channel SIC Noticias in 2016. “A head of government, to manage a country, has to make decisions that please some and displease others and sometimes that pleases almost no one.”

Still, Guterres was growing increasingly comfortable on the international stage. In the first half of 2000, Portugal held the rotating presidency of the European Union, giving its prime minister a prominent diplomatic role. Guterres was valued for his ability to mediate among competing governments and to remain composed during tense negotiations.

“At the European Council, I remember a conflict between Jacques Chirac and Helmut Kohl over one issue,” Francisco Seixas da Costa, a Portuguese diplomat who served as Guterres’s European affairs secretary, told the Guardian.

“Guterres asked for the floor. I was sitting next to him; I was afraid it might be naive. But he took the floor and made a proposal that covered both their interests and it was a success. It worked. He had a fantastic capacity to moderate and create links and bridges.”

In late 2000, EU leaders were negotiating rules for expanding the bloc from 15 members to as many as 27. The central question was how to distribute voting power in a much larger bloc. The major powers — Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Spain — wanted greater weight in the EU Council, while smaller countries feared they would be reduced to bystanders.

Guterres called the initial proposal an “institutional coup d’etat” and joined Belgium and other small states in resisting it — adding pressure that led to a compromise.

At home, however, his minority government was struggling, and in December 2001 the socialists suffered major setbacks in local elections. Guterres accepted the blame and a little over two years into his second term, he resigned to prevent the country from falling into what he called a “political swamp”.

According to Costa Pinto, Guterres resigned partly because his government was in such a weak position that he would have been forced to compromise his principles, for example, by greenlighting austerity measures he disagreed with. Still, he was seen as abandoning his post in a time of need and was harshly criticised by the socialists.

“He was also accused of resigning [because] he was not proud to lead the country in an already difficult financial situation,” the historian added.

After leaving office, Guterres quietly resumed volunteering, teaching free maths lessons several times a week in the deprived Lisbon neighbourhood of Quinta do Mocho. The former PM avoided publicity, refusing to allow reporters to photograph him or his pupils.

“That’s the kind of person he is,” Goulao said about Guterres’s private volunteerism.

“He’s very involved in social issues. He’s Catholic and he practises the demands of his beliefs very well.”

In 2001, Guterres remarried, this time to Catarina Vaz Pinto, a former secretary of state for culture.

Meanwhile, with a keen interest in the plight of refugees, Guterres was considering what to do after his political career when the international stage beckoned. Kofi Annan, the then-UN secretary-general, nominated Guterres to become the next UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in 2005. His experience as the founder of the Portuguese Refugee Council put him ahead of the other candidates and in June of that year he took on his first UN posting. Four days later, he was at a camp for refugees displaced by the Lord’s Resistance Army in Uganda, the first of countless field trips to hotspots around the globe.

The job, which he held until the end of 2015, would show Guterres that refugee protection rarely existed without political involvement. He repeatedly had to defend people who were fleeing violence while also persuading governments — often under intense domestic pressure — that forced returns were unlawful and impractical. Just before the end of his tenure at UNHCR, that tension confronted him in Kenya.

The refugee crises

Early on April 3, 2015, four armed men stepped onto the campus of Garissa University College in eastern Kenya and opened fire, going from building to building and killing students they identified as Christians. They killed 148 people before Kenyan soldiers cornered and killed them in a female dormitory.

Following the bloodbath, Kenyan authorities singled out Dadaab refugee camp, a large complex in the country’s northeast, as a security threat. They claimed that the al-Shabaab armed group was using the camps to recruit and plan attacks. Unless the UN helped close Dadaab, Kenyan officials were threatening to shut it down themselves and return its Somali residents to the country they had fled because of war.

As the UN refugee chief, Guterres was responsible for protecting the Somali refugees in Dadaab and ensuring that any return to Somalia was voluntary and safe. He boarded a plane from his headquarters in Geneva to Mogadishu to meet the Somali president before flying to Nairobi to speak with his Kenyan counterpart. They reached an understanding to keep the camp open.

Internally, at UNHCR, the former Portuguese premier implemented reforms to improve the organisation’s response capacity and efficiency, while reducing its presence in Geneva. The organisation still managed to grow and Guterres persuaded donors to part with more funding while he dispatched staffers into the field. Through the Global Protection Cluster, the UNHCR broadened the scope of those under its care to include those escaping natural disasters.

“It's not by coincidence that he started an international career as commissioner for the refugees of the United Nations,” Costa Pinto said.

Guterres’s efforts were closely aligned with Pope Francis, the reformist head of the Catholic Church and a strong advocate for refugees.

“That’s where, I think, his vocation as a politician is clearly represented: humanism, peace, conflict resolution and of course, this is very much connected with political Catholicism. Actually, firstly, that dominates his career.”

That commitment was also evident to those who worked with him. In 2012, he appointed Hollywood actress Angelina Jolie as a special envoy to raise awareness of humanitarian crises.

“I spend a lot of time with him on the ground and have been able to see not only his compassion for refugees and their families, but also how tirelessly he fights on behalf of the UN to protect these people,” Jolie told SIC in a 2016 interview.

“Guterres does much more than meets the eye. He is relentless in his commitment," she added.

But he has also faced criticism. In 2015, as Europe struggled with its largest refugee influx in decades, the body of three-year-old Syrian Alan Kurdi washed up on a Turkish beach. The image became a symbol of a crisis marked by hostile border guards, squalid tent cities and chaotic reception centres. Critics argued that the UN system had failed to push European governments to share responsibility and create safe routes for refugees.

Guterres, however, was publicly demanding a far more ambitious response. He called for a mandatory EU relocation programme for up to 200,000 refugees, greater support for Greece and expanded resettlement and humanitarian programmes.

During his visits to Washington, DC, as the head of UNHCR, Guterres reportedly spent his spare time perusing Politics & Prose and other local bookshops.

Described by former Portuguese Finance Minister Guilherme de Oliveira Martins as possessing an “unbeatable knowledge of world history”, Guterres has developed a reputation as an intellectual who enjoys conversations on a variety of topics — from ancient Greece and Middle Eastern culture to opera and geography. He is also said to have a sweet tooth, with a particular weakness for Portuguese custard tarts, which he reportedly took with him onboard official flights.

Back home, the Socialist Party wanted Guterres to run for national office again, this time as president, but he wasn’t interested.

Then, in December 2015, the Portuguese government received a letter from the UN, asking if it was interested in presenting a candidate to succeed the outgoing Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon. Ideally, the UN advised, the candidate would be a woman from Eastern Europe.

Portugal ignored the advice and presented Guterres as its candidate instead, emphasising his experience as head of the Portuguese government, his diplomacy on behalf of East Timor and his handling of many crises during his decade-long leadership of UNHCR.

Back home, Guterres enjoyed bipartisan backing.

“In Portugal, the centre-right and the centre-left always support each other when their politicians apply to major international positions,” explained Costa Pinto.

“It’s an old policy of the main two parties [and] the typical policy of a small country: one wants to have a not very ideological profile in international terms.”

In the end, Guterres’s personal charm and humour, and because he was seen as someone both Moscow and Washington could work with, made him the frontrunner for the position. On October 13, 2016, aged 67, he was approved by the UN General Assembly to succeed Ban Ki-moon.

The senior statesman

On taking the reins as UN Secretary-General, Guterres pledged “a surge in diplomacy for peace”. In practice, of course, this was far easier said than done.

Like at the UNHCR, Guterres implemented institutional reforms as UN chief and his early years were shaped by protracted wars in Syria and Yemen, the Rohingya crisis in Myanmar, the renewed conflict in Libya, the anti-multilateralist approach of Donald Trump’s first presidential term and the pandemic. Security Council divisions, however, limited what he could achieve when it came to the biggest conflicts.

Then, on February 24, 2022, Ukrainians and Russians awoke to news that their countries were in a full-scale war. Russian tanks rolled over Ukraine’s eastern frontier while terrified civilians sought shelter in Kyiv’s Metro.

The UN Security Council convened and Guterres condemned the invasion. “In the name of humanity, bring your troops back to Russia,” he implored President Vladimir Putin, who ignored the plea.

On April 26 , Guterres met with Putin to discuss evacuation routes from besieged areas, such as the city of Mariupol, and later that week he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Guterres’s diplomacy saw some initial success. In 2022, he brokered the Black Sea grain deal, enabling the safe passage of Ukrainian ships carrying grain exports from the country’s southern ports, as well as Russian vessels carrying food and fertiliser.

But beyond these humanitarian initiatives, he’s been less successful in handling the war’s thorny politics. In 2024, Zelenskyy spurned Guterres’s planned visit to Kyiv after the UN chief attended the BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) summit in Kazan, Russia, where he shook Putin’s hand and called for a “just peace”.

By this point, Putin was wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes. Guterres’s decision to attend the summit and meet Putin drew sharp criticism from Ukrainian officials, European leaders and human rights groups.

Then, on October 7, 2023, another conflict erupted as Hamas-led fighters launched a surprise attack on Israel, killing more than 1,100 Israelis and foreign nationals, including hundreds of revellers at a music festival. The Israeli response was a heavy bombardment of Gaza, including attacks on hospitals, refugee camps and designated “safe zones”. An estimated 75,000 Palestinians had been violently killed by early 2025 and the UN’s independent Commission of Inquiry concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejects.

Two weeks after the initial attack, Guterres drew sharp condemnation from Israeli leaders for saying October 7th “did not happen in a vacuum” – referring to the blockade of Gaza and the ongoing occupation of the West Bank – and calling for a ceasefire. Guterres clarified his remarks, stressing that “the grievances of the Palestinian people cannot justify the appalling attacks by Hamas,” as he kept pushing for a ceasefire.

On December 6, 2023, Guterres invoked the rarely used Article 99 of the UN Charter, bringing to the attention of the UN’s 15-member Security Council “any issue that may aggravate existing threats to the maintenance of international peace and security”, calling on its members to “avert a humanitarian catastrophe” in Gaza and press for a ceasefire. Two days later, the United States vetoed the resolution.

In October 2024, Israel declared Guterres persona non grata, barring him from the country after accusing him of failing to “unequivocally condemn” Iran’s missile attack on Israel. This deepened the rift between Israel and the UN, limiting his ability to engage with Israeli leaders.

So Guterres has failed to make significant progress in Gaza or Ukraine, two of the major conflicts of his tenure. Part of that is due to the natural constraints of the job, having to maintain a commitment to international law while remaining a credible broker between global powers. He cannot impose settlements without the cooperation of the parties involved and the backing of major powers.

The Security Council is often divided by the competing interests of Russia, China and the Western powers, and the UN’s work has been complicated by governments — including the United States under Trump — that have challenged multilateral institutions or disputed the authority of international legal bodies.

A 2021 International Crisis Group assessment found that some officials involved in Middle East mediation viewed Guterres as reluctant to expend his personal political capital on risky peace initiatives. The assessment reflected his approach before the Gaza war and the invasion of Ukraine, but it perhaps explains his style of relying on envoys, humanitarian advocacy and quiet diplomacy rather than high-stakes personal mediation.

Others say that while he takes a keen interest in crises worldwide, he can rely too much on world leaders’ interpretation of events. During Ethiopia’s Tigray war, for instance, he publicly relayed Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s assurance that Eritrean troops had not entered Tigrayan territory, apart from a disputed border area. Abiy later acknowledged that Eritrean forces had entered Tigray.

Guterres has also been cautious about deploying traditional UN Blue Helmet missions, questioning whether they can operate effectively without a viable political process and sufficient security. That caution was visible in Haiti. Asked to consider a wider range of UN options as gangs tightened their grip on Port-au-Prince, Guterres ruled out deploying a conventional Blue Helmet mission. Instead, he proposed that the UN fund and operate a logistics office to support the Kenyan-led multinational force while strengthening the UN’s political mission and providing limited assistance to Haiti’s police.

“Before Guterres came to office, there had been a steady expansion of UN peacekeeping,” explained Daniel Forti, a UN specialist at Crisis Group.

“There was a worrying trend that a number of missions – including previous ones deployed to Somalia and the current one in the Central African Republic and the DRC – were being asked to impose peace in places where there was no peace to keep.”

“Guterres was incredibly sceptical of this type of approach and sought to encourage others to take on those responsibilities and have a much narrower interpretation of what UN Blue Helmets can actually do in certain types of conflicts,” he added.

When it comes to actual peace-making, Guterres prefers the UN to refrain from taking decisions on behalf of locals and instead delegates to regional players. In the case of Ethiopia, he wanted the African Union (AU) to take a more prominent role and called for more funding for AU efforts.

His reluctance to engage more fully may stem from personal experience. In 2017, the secretary-general took part in Cyprus reunification talks that collapsed, leaving him “visibly despondent.” Likewise, in 2019, he visited Libya to try to bring the warring sides to the negotiating table, only for rebels to mount an offensive on Tripoli. Before leaving the country, Guterres said Libya left him with “a heavy heart”.

According to Forti, these experiences may have also left him wary.

“At first, when he came into office, he emphasised a very strong agenda on conflict prevention,” Forti said.

“But after a few instances where Guterres tried to get personally involved in peace-making efforts, including in Cyprus, he got burned quite quickly and didn’t show an inclination to persevere with political processes over a long period of time.”

Any hope of quick wins or decisive outcomes proved a lot harder.

“From that moment, he’s shown less and less inclination to be directly involved,” Forti added.

Rather than finding solutions to conflicts, he says, Guterres instead focuses on humanitarian relief, ensuring lifesaving assistance reaches civilians.

Guterres himself has admitted that world peace is “a Sisyphean task”, referring to the mythical Greek king cursed to keep pushing a boulder up a hill only for it to roll back down again. Perhaps drawing a lesson from that, Guterres has channelled some of his energy into areas where he felt he could make more of a difference – notably, the climate crisis.

“Half of humanity is in the danger zone from floods, droughts, extreme storms and wildfires,” he told world leaders in 2022. “No nation is immune. Yet we continue to feed our fossil fuel addiction.”

“We have a choice – collective action or collective suicide. It is in our hands.”

Paloma Costa, a 34-year-old Brazilian climate activist who served on Guterres’s 2020 inaugural Youth Advisory Group on Climate Change, said the secretary-general sees global warming as a major problem facing society and has actively supported youth-led movements fighting for their future.

“He has been very committed to paying attention to the [problem], to listening to young people who have been taking on this agenda for ourselves and putting up our voices strongly against decisions that are destroying our common environment.”

The advisory group’s responsibilities included compiling reports and demands from young people across the globe and summarising them for Guterres.

“He made sure there was pressure on the global level because for a long time, the climate discussions were not advancing very much,” Costa said.

In doing so, Guterres has emphasised that poorer, underdeveloped nations in the Global South suffer the most from environmental catastrophes and that wealthier countries must take on their fair share of the responsibility. He has called for windfall taxes on the fossil fuel industry, telling global delegates in 2022 that “polluters must pay”. He also praised the establishment of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), agreed to at a 2022 climate conference, to help vulnerable countries cope with climate emergencies. But these initiatives have yet to be applied at the scale needed and the FRLD remains severely underfunded.

“Even though he didn’t always have an immediate answer, I always felt embraced because he always made sure we were understood and taken seriously, and there was always a follow-up to let us know if something could not be resolved, why it could not be resolved,” Costa said.

Consistent with his non-confrontational approach, however, Guterres has stopped short of naming specific parties or countries unduly responsible for the warming planet.

Guterres has also warned against the unchecked development of artificial intelligence (AI). Since 2023, he has sought to make AI governance a central UN concern, pressing governments to develop international safeguards and give developing countries a greater voice in shaping the technology. He has also called for a legally binding ban on lethal autonomous weapons.

In July, he warned that AI could become one of humanity’s greatest opportunities — or one of its greatest dangers — depending on whether governments and technology firms agree to govern it effectively.

Making history

With his second five-year term as UN chief ending on December 31, how will the world see Guterres’s legacy in the years to come? Will he be remembered for his handling of acute crises or for his climate advocacy?

“The UN’s relevance has certainly taken a hit in recent years, especially when members of the Security Council have not shown interest in following core principles of the Charter,” said Forti.

But the UN specialist doesn’t think Guterres fared worse than others would have under the same circumstances.

“Many secretaries-general would struggle with some of the same fundamental tensions that Guterres has,” Forti said.

While he acknowledges that Guterres has lost political capital with some states, Forti still sees a positive legacy for the UN head.

“History books will remember Guterres more favourably for the work he’s done, both on the climate change agenda and on bringing the artificial intelligence agenda into the multilateral sphere.”

Guterres, he says, has been “shining the beacon” on the need for international rules before the technology outruns governments’ ability to control it.

“These are incredibly global-changing issues that have not always been the easiest politically to corral member states to think about, now or in the future, and the fact that Guterres has been consistent in putting these on the agenda [will have] far more positive and long-term ramifications than we can see right now.”

articles.body:
Croatia’s Hajduk Split hosted Ajax on Thursday, but chants for pre-World War II regime precede UEFA Europa League game.

Croatian leaders have slammed pro-Nazi and anti-Semitic chants by Hajduk Split football fans before their UEFA Conference League match against Ajax, while Israel’s embassy voiced shock.

Groups of Hajduk Split fans, known as the Torcida, marched through the coastal town of Split before Thursday’s match chanting: “Crush the Jews”, “Rise up Adolf (Hitler)” and “Let’s go Ustasha”, referring to the country’s World War II pro-Nazi regime, local media reported.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items

- list 1 of 4Man Utd veering towards crisis as Man City cloud hangs over Premier League

- list 2 of 4Man United’s Martinez apologises for outburst after talks with Carrick

- list 3 of 4Man United’s Martinez takes to social media to defend his criticism of club

- list 4 of 4What led Manchester United’s Martinez to meltdown in Madrid – all to know

Dozens of fans were detained before Thursday’s match for violence. During the match, Torcida fans set off flares and other pyrotechnics in the stands, forcing more than a 10-minute stoppage.

An investigation was opened into the pro-Nazi chants and suspects are being detained, police said.

President Zoran Milanovic in a Friday statement condemned the incident as “unacceptable and shameful”.

He urged swift action against the perpetrators to “show that there is no place in Croatia for the glorification of Nazism and Ustasha ideology”.

Israel’s embassy in Zagreb said on X it was “deeply shocked by the serious antisemitic incident that took place in Split and condemns it in the strongest possible terms”.

Conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic also condemned “messages of anti-Semitism … completely at odds with the values we want to uphold in Croatian society”.

Hajduk Split, who won the game 2-1, in a statement apologised to UEFA and Ajax who “witnessed scenes which we do not want Europe to remember”, while the Croatian football federation also condemned the incident.

Croatia’s ultra-nationalist hardcore supporters have tainted the country’s image for years, notably by chanting pro-fascist slogans and displaying Ustasha symbols.

The Ustasha regime killed and persecuted hundreds of thousands of ethnic Serbs, Jews, Roma and antifascist Croatians.

Croatia were docked a point by UEFA after their fans painted a swastika on the pitch in Split in 2015, before a Euro 2016 qualifier with Italy.

The perpetrators were never found.

In recent years, the country has seen a growing tolerance for its pro-Nazi past, and critics accuse authorities of failing to sanction the use of Ustasha emblems.

articles.title: La Audiencia de Madrid ordena investigar si Vito Quiles coaccionó a Begoña Gómez
articles.summary: El tribunal anula la decisión de un juzgado de Majadahonda de archivar la denuncia que presentó la esposa del presidente del Gobierno contra el agitador
articles.preview: La Audiencia Provincial de Madrid ha anulado la decisión de un juzgado de Majadahonda de archivar la denuncia que presentó la esposa del presidente del Gobierno, Begoña Gómez, contra el agitador ultra Víctor Zoppellari Quiles, conocido como Vito Quiles , por unos hechos ocurridos el pasado 29 de abril, cuando se encontraba en un restaurante en Las Rozas (Madrid).
articles.body:
La Audiencia Provincial de Madrid ha anulado la decisión de un juzgado de Majadahonda de archivar la denuncia que presentó la esposa del presidente del Gobierno, Begoña Gómez, contra el agitador ultra Víctor Zoppellari Quiles, conocido como Vito Quiles , por unos hechos ocurridos el pasado 29 de abril, cuando se encontraba en un restaurante en Las Rozas (Madrid). El tribunal considera prematura la decisión del juez de instrucción y ordena reabrir la causa para investigar si los hechos denunciados encajan en un delito de coacciones, ya que el denunciado buscó “deliberadamente” coincidir con la mujer de Pedro Sánchez mientras ella desarrollaba una actividad privada en un espacio público.

articles.summary: AGI - Riforme interne, difesa comune , sistema finanziario. Tutto con la dovuta velocità. Questi i punti cardine offerti dal Presidente della Repubblica, Sergio Mattarella , agli omologhi di 11 Paesi europei riuniti a Lubiana per la ventunesima riunione del Gruppo Arraiolos . Una riunione sulla quale, stando a quanto si apprende, aleggia l' ombra della Russia. Mattarella, riequilibrare la postura della Russia Lo stesso Presidente Mattarella ha sollecitato a procedere con slancio verso una maggiore interoperabilità degli strumenti militari dei Paesi dell' Unione in chiave di difesa comune e di rafforzamento della Nato, gli unici mezzi per "riequilibrare" la postura della Russia nel vecchio continente. Mattarella, definito dalla presidente slovena Pirc Musar “il m embro più anziano e rispettato ”, ha sottolineato che "non occorrono molte parole riguardo alla necessità della difesa comune , procedendo con determinazione e velocità alla interoperabilità dei nostri strumenti militari, sia perché condizione indispensabile per la difesa comune sia per rafforzare la Nato sul versante europeo, per ripristinare l'equilibrio rispetto alla postura della Russia. Equilibrio che, nella storia, è sempre stato la garanzia della pace, vanificando tentazioni di aggressività". Allargare l'Unione al Balcani Occidentali Assieme a questo, il Capo dello Stato ha sollecitato un rapido allargamento dell'Unione ai Balcani Occidentali , ma anche a Ucraina e Moldova. Un processo che deve procedere di pari passo con quello delle r iforme interne di un'Unione troppo lenta - è il ragionamento del Presidente - nell'assumere quelle decisioni che richiede il continuo mutamento del quadro internazionale. "﻿﻿L'interesse della generazione di oggi e di quelle future richiede che si prosegua con determinazione con le riforme interne necessarie", avverte. "Servono decisioni più snelle e veloci" "﻿﻿Essendo un anziano presidente - purtroppo non soltanto come incarico - questo è il dodicesimo incontro di Arrajolos cui partecipo", ricorda il Capo dello Stato: "In questi dodici anni ho visto crescere progressivamente la consapevolezza che l'Unione ha indispensabile bisogno di modalità di decisione più snelle e veloci ". Per il Presidente, infatti, "senza velocità di decisioni questi problemi, nella vita internazionale, verrebbero decisi da altri soggetti e in Europa ne subiremmo passivamente gli effetti". Parole che arrivano mentre i leader dei Ventisette riuniti ha Bruxelles affrontano il nodo del caro energia, la tenuta della competitività e la revisione del quadro finanziario pluriennale, con un’attenzione particolare al sostegno militare e infrastrutturale all’Ucraina in vista dell’inverno. "Il quadro finanziario della Ue sia ambizioso" "Un elemento decisivo è rappresentato dal negoziato sul Quadro Finanziario Pluriennale dell'Unione", avverte Mattarella, "perché le scelte che compiremo definiranno non solo la distribuzione delle risorse europee, ma anche il livello di ambizione con cui l'Europa intende affrontare le trasformazioni in atto. Mi auguro che sia adeguatamente ambizioso". Più in generale, poi, "è necessario completare il sistema finanziario dell'Unione" per poter reggere il confronto con altre economie: "Non possiamo restare a lungo con un e dificio complesso incompleto . Sarà di grande difficoltà trovare le intese per approdarvi, ma è indispensabile", è il monito del Presidente della Repubblica". La chiosa suona come un invito alla fiducia diretto agli omologhi europei: "Sembra che i nostri concittadini avvertano - più di alcuni commentatori - quanto nell'Unione stiamo facendo per presentare al mondo e concretamente realizzare un modello di pace e convivenza collaborativa. La rete di accordi di libero scambio che l'Unione ha realizzato e sta ulteriormente sviluppando con altre grandi aree del mondo - dal Canada al Mercosur, dal Giappone all'India, all'Australia e altre aree - produce interessi condivisi e obiettivi comuni, garanzia di pace". Quello che rappresenta, in ultima analisi, il modello multilaterale messo in crisi dal proliferare dei conflitti. "Un modello alternativo a quello degli scontri, dei contrasti commerciali o addirittura bellici", conclude Mattarella.

"﻿﻿L'interesse della generazione di oggi e di quelle future richiede che si prosegua con determinazione con le riforme interne necessarie", avverte. "Servono decisioni più snelle e veloci" "﻿﻿Essendo un anziano presidente - purtroppo non soltanto come incarico - questo è il dodicesimo incontro di Arrajolos cui partecipo", ricorda il Capo dello Stato: "In questi dodici anni ho visto crescere progressivamente la consapevolezza che l'Unione ha indispensabile bisogno di modalità di decisione più snelle e veloci ".

Per il Presidente, infatti, "senza velocità di decisioni questi problemi, nella vita internazionale, verrebbero decisi da altri soggetti e in Europa ne subiremmo passivamente gli effetti". Parole che arrivano mentre i leader dei Ventisette riuniti ha Bruxelles affrontano il nodo del caro energia, la tenuta della competitività e la revisione del quadro finanziario pluriennale, con un’attenzione particolare al sostegno militare e infrastrutturale all’Ucraina in vista dell’inverno.

"Il quadro finanziario della Ue sia ambizioso" "Un elemento decisivo è rappresentato dal negoziato sul Quadro Finanziario Pluriennale dell'Unione", avverte Mattarella, "perché le scelte che compiremo definiranno non solo la distribuzione delle risorse europee, ma anche il livello di ambizione con cui l'Europa intende affrontare le trasformazioni in atto. Mi auguro che sia adeguatamente ambizioso".

Più in generale, poi, "è necessario completare il sistema finanziario dell'Unione" per poter reggere il confronto con altre economie: "Non possiamo restare a lungo con un e dificio complesso incompleto . Sarà di grande difficoltà trovare le intese per approdarvi, ma è indispensabile", è il monito del Presidente della Repubblica". La chiosa suona come un invito alla fiducia diretto agli omologhi europei: "Sembra che i nostri concittadini avvertano - più di alcuni commentatori - quanto nell'Unione stiamo facendo per presentare al mondo e concretamente realizzare un modello di pace e convivenza collaborativa.

La rete di accordi di libero scambio che l'Unione ha realizzato e sta ulteriormente sviluppando con altre grandi aree del mondo - dal Canada al Mercosur, dal Giappone all'India, all'Australia e altre aree - produce interessi condivisi e obiettivi comuni, garanzia di pace". Quello che rappresenta, in ultima analisi, il modello multilaterale messo in crisi dal proliferare dei conflitti. "Un modello alternativo a quello degli scontri, dei contrasti commerciali o addirittura bellici", conclude Mattarella.

articles.title: Il presente distopico dei Fontaines D.C.
articles.summary: Il nuovo album della band irlandese insegue ancora atmosfere cinematografiche, ma stavolta si addentra nell’oscurità con più convinzione. E ha le canzoni giuste per farlo
articles.preview: In una delle scene più belle di Blade runner il protagonista Rick Deckard, interpretato da Harrison Ford, fa una serie di domande a una donna chiamata Rachael per capire se è una persona vera o una replicante. Dopo il test, le rivela che i suoi ricordi d’infanzia appartengono alla nipote del direttore della Tyrell Corporation, l’azienda che costruisce gli umanoidi. “Dai, era solo un brutto scherzo, non sei veramente una replicante, vai a casa”, dice Deckard quando si rende conto che Rachael sta piangendo.
articles.body:
In una delle scene più belle di Blade runner il protagonista Rick Deckard, interpretato da Harrison Ford, fa una serie di domande a una donna chiamata Rachael per capire se è una persona vera o una replicante. Dopo il test, le rivela che i suoi ricordi d’infanzia appartengono alla nipote del direttore della Tyrell Corporation, l’azienda che costruisce gli umanoidi. “Dai, era solo un brutto scherzo, non sei veramente una replicante, vai a casa”, dice Deckard quando si rende conto che Rachael sta piangendo. Ma è troppo tardi, ormai la verità è venuta fuori. I replicanti immaginati dal film del 1982 di Ridley Scott – un capolavoro che ancora oggi parla al nostro presente – sono umani creati con tecniche di bioingegneria e dotati appunto di ricordi impiantati da persone reali.

Il modo in cui Grian Chatten, il cantante e principale paroliere dei Fontaines D.C., analizza il nostro presente non è poi così lontano dalla distopia futurista di Scott. Le canzoni del nuovo album della band irlandese, Dopamine chamber, sembrano dirci che in un certo senso anche noi viviamo come replicanti, plasmati dagli algoritmi e dai social media. E che le scariche di dopamina che provengono dagli schermi dei nostri telefoni sostituiscono le esperienze in prima persona.

“Camera della dopamina / sto solo cercando di alleviare il dolore”, canta Chatten in One man, uno dei pezzi più riusciti del disco. Nel brano, una struggente dichiarazione d’amore sotto un “cielo sporco e rosso” – che potrebbe essere quello colorato dagli incendi sempre più frequenti sul nostro pianeta, ma anche il cielo ocra del sequel di Blade runner firmato da Denis Villeneuve – chi parla dice all’altra persona: “If i failed you, i’m not sorry, i’m only one man”. Se ho sbagliato non ti chiedo scusa, sono solo un uomo. La quasi disperata dichiarazione d’umanità è una delle chiavi ricorrenti dell’album, ma una delle cose interessanti di Dopamine chamber è l’ostinato romanticismo presente nella voce (le parti cantate sono state registrate in una casa a Palermo) e nelle parole di Chatten, che fa da contraltare a una musica sintetica, glaciale.

Intendiamoci, con i Fontaines D.C. (che saranno in Italia per tre date nei prossimi mesi) non siamo mai di fronte alla sperimentazione sonora pura, ci troviamo pur sempre nell’ambito del pop-rock da classifica. Eppure la carriera della band di Dublino, sempre meno irlandese e sempre più cosmopolita, continua a regalare spunti interessanti. Le chitarre nervose degli esordi, che sostenevano un Chatten più verboso e vicino allo spoken-word, sono tenute più sotto controllo (anche se emergono qua e là, come nell’intensa Happy for you, che funzionerà benissimo ai concerti e sembra un omaggio ai Cure più orecchiabili) e il suono della band oggi somiglia a quello dei Depeche Mode (nel brano Mimesis) o perfino a quello dei Joy Division, come succede nel sontuoso pezzo d’apertura Six shot morning, costruito su un basso distorto che sembra un tributo a Peter Hook e su un azzeccato crescendo di batteria e sintetizzatori alla Vangelis (e torniamo ancora a Blade runner). Ad ascoltare quella voce baritonale, poi, non può che venire in mente Ian Curtis.

Già con il disco precedente, Romance, i Fontaines D.C. si erano allontanati dalle atmosfere plumbee e dublinesi degli esordi. Quel lavoro era attraversato da un’inquietudine più contemporanea, ma anche dalla voglia di parlare una lingua più universale e pop. Non mancavano i guizzi (su tutti il singolo Starburster, ma anche la ballata In the modern world), ma Romance aveva il difetto di cercare la consacrazione agli occhi del grande pubblico in modo troppo evidente. Dopamine chamber, invece, si rifugia nell’inquietudine e nell’introspezione. Insegue ancora atmosfere da grande schermo (quei “cinematic feelings” evocati dal singolo Marianne), ma stavolta si addentra nell’oscurità con più convinzione, con un occhio a David Lynch e un orecchio al rock degli anni ottanta.

È come se i Fontaines D.C. avessero portato Romance alle sue estreme conseguenze. La fortuna è che, stavolta, avevano per le mani le canzoni giuste per spingersi oltre. L’unico passaggio totalmente a vuoto è, paradossalmente, quello che sulla carta sembrava infallibile: la ballata orchestrale e morriconiana Where is gone?. Il pezzo, a detta della band ispirato anche da Se telefonando, ospita addirittura la popstar spagnola Rosalía, che duetta con Chatten un po’ come Kylie Minogue fece con Nick Cave in Where the wild roses grow. Peccato che la canzone, per quanto ben arrangiata, sia davvero telefonata.

Nel finale, con la doppietta formata da Japan e Intimate, la band si risolleva, portando il disco su un ottimo livello complessivo. E nell’ultimo brano, ambientato a Venezia, una città galleggiante in cui “la deco-dance non ha fine”, Chatten canta in modo ossessivo: “Intimate it’s all that’s real”. Come a dire, solo nel nostro intimo, fuori dal digitale, è nascosta la verità. Lontano dai ricordi impiantati dagli altri.

articles.title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
articles.summary: Over the past year there has been a stark rise in anti-government activists deported to Russia from the EU and US where they were seeking refuge.
articles.preview: Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum. "It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia. Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians.
articles.body:
Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.

"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.

Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.

US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.

In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.

The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.

"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."

Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.

"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"

Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.

Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.

One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.

"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.

And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.

Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.

"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.

Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.

Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.

Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.

Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.

Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.

"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."

He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.

"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".

Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.

"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."

The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."

The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.

The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.

Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.

Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".

Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.

The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned.

"We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!"

"We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."

Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.

The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.

For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.

There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.

Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge â or send them back.

articles.title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
articles.summary: France's prime minister has suggested that student anger is being weaponised, as the unions and other protesters prepare to take to the streets too.
articles.preview: The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe. Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs. For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets. This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
articles.body:
The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.

Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.

For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.

This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.

Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.

France's Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.

The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.

Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.

The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.

"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.

So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?

Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.

Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?

"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.

She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.

"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."

"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.

"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."

"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.

Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.

But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.

France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.

I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.

They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.

"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."

None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.

The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.

- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger

- Published8 October

They are part of a defiant French tradition.

Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."

("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")

Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."

Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.

Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.

This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.

France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.

Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.

At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.

"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."

Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the Âbiggest general strike in French Âhistory. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.

Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.

"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.

"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.

But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.

Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.

For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's â¬11bn contribution to the EU's budget.

There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.

France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Gulf.

Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.

In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.

Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.

But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.

"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.

"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."

For France to progress, she says, that has to change.

The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."

In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.

"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."

Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.

She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.

Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".

"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."

I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."

"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."

"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."

It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.

But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.
